intro: Two sets of theories. The ten course theses are the explanations the Cowell 103 seminar examined, one per session. The primer is the syllabus's Appendix V, a catalog of 60 theories proposed in the first years after the assassination, many first collected by Edward Jay Epstein for Esquire (1966), from serious forensic disputes to the frankly absurd. Summaries are in our own words; page numbers refer to the syllabus PDF.

theses.name: Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone (the lone-gunman theory)
theses.summary: Oswald, firing three shots from the sixth floor of the Book Depository, killed the President and wounded Governor Connally, with no help and no one behind him. The conclusion of the Warren Commission.

theses.name: The CIA assassinated JFK
theses.summary: Presented as the credible facts that challenge the single-bullet explanation, pointing to elements of the CIA, its anti-Castro operations and its contacts with Oswald.

theses.name: The HSCA's "probable conspiracy" and Blakey & Billings: the Mob, using Trafficante-connected anti-Castro exiles
theses.summary: The House Select Committee concluded in 1979 that Kennedy was probably killed as a result of a conspiracy; its chief counsel G. Robert Blakey and writer Richard Billings argued organized crime was behind it, working through anti-Castro Cubans tied to Santo Trafficante.

theses.name: Jim Garrison's On the Trail of the Assassins: the trial of Clay Shaw
theses.summary: New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison's case that a conspiracy involving Clay Shaw, David Ferrie and anti-Castro and intelligence figures in New Orleans planned the assassination. Shaw was acquitted in 1969.

theses.name: The Cuban "backfire": Johnny Roselli's theory that Fidel Castro killed JFK
theses.summary: U.S. plots to kill Castro, run with Mafia help, backfired: Castro (or people turned by Cuba) retaliated against Kennedy. The theory was promoted by mobster Johnny Roselli.

theses.name: The Watergate burglary connection: Santo Trafficante's "S-Force" killed JFK
theses.summary: A team tied to Trafficante and to men later caught in the Watergate burglary carried out the assassination, an account presented to Sheehan by Trafficante's attorney Frank Ragano.

theses.name: David Lifton's Best Evidence: "the floodgates open"
theses.summary: The President's body was altered before the Bethesda autopsy to hide shots from the front, so the official medical evidence cannot be trusted.

theses.name: Seven Days in May: Curtis LeMay and the Joint Chiefs staged a military coup
theses.summary: Military leaders opposed to Kennedy's policies on Cuba, the Soviet Union and Vietnam, led by Air Force Chief of Staff Curtis LeMay, had him killed. Presented with John Judge of the Coalition on Political Assassinations.

theses.name: The KGB killed JFK
theses.summary: Soviet intelligence, which had Oswald under its eye during his defection, was behind the assassination.

theses.name: Sheehan & Billings: the Rulers of the Realm
theses.summary: The instructor's own thesis, from a book then forthcoming with Richard Billings. The syllabus does not spell it out; the course's network map points to a coalition of financiers, intelligence officers, military figures and organized-crime and exile operatives.

primer.name: Single-bullet theory
primer.proponents: The Warren Commission, especially counsel Arlen Specter (who developed it in March 1964) and Norman Redlich
primer.claim: One shot missed (a fragment or debris wounded James Tague); one bullet passed through Kennedy's neck and caused all of Connally's wounds; the third hit Kennedy's head.
primer.selling: The only way a single gunman could have done it: the film allows at most about 1.8 seconds between the first possible hit on Kennedy and the last possible first hit on Connally, too short to fire the rifle twice.
primer.drawback: The holes in the President's shirt and jacket, and the FBI's account, place the back wound below the shoulder, an unlikely point for a bullet from above to exit at the throat.

primer.name: FBI theory
primer.claim: The first bullet entered Kennedy's back only a finger's length and fell out during heart massage; the second hit Connally; the third hit Kennedy's head; all from the Depository.
primer.selling: Matches the clothing holes, the autopsy sketch and Secret Service testimony placing the back wound well below the collar.
primer.drawback: Separate bullets for Kennedy and Connally imply a second gunman, it can't account for the shot that wounded Tague, and it contradicts the Commission's autopsy findings.

primer.name: Head movement theory
primer.claim: Comparing Zapruder frames 313 and 316, the head snaps back and to the left, implying the fatal shot came from the grassy knoll, possibly a dumdum bullet Oswald's rifle couldn't fire.

primer.name: Early hit theory
primer.claim: Kennedy was first hit between Zapruder frames 190 and 210, when a tree blocked the Depository window, so the shot came from elsewhere.

primer.name: Missing-frame theory
primer.claim: Frames 208–211 are missing from the Commission's published frames and the Archives slides, with splice marks at 207 and 212, suggesting a shot in that interval was suppressed.
primer.drawback: Life magazine's original film is reportedly complete and shows no hit in those frames; the Archives copies may simply have been damaged.

primer.name: Traffic sign theory
primer.claim: Marks visible on a traffic sign from frame 212 to 221 were caused by a bullet strike that doesn't fit Oswald's timing; the sign was removed soon afterwards.

primer.name: Entry wound theory
primer.proponents: Mark Lane, Thomas Buchanan, Joachim Joesten and others
primer.claim: Dallas doctors' early statements describe the throat wound as an entrance, so a shot came from in front: first the overpass, later the grassy knoll.
primer.selling: Fits the doctors' first statements and the small size of the throat wound.
primer.drawback: Doesn't say where that bullet went (no exit wound or bullet was found), so it requires the autopsy evidence to have been altered.

primer.name: Over the fence theory
primer.proponents: UPI's Maurice Schonfeld, Jack Fox and Burt Reinhardt
primer.claim: An enlargement of a frame of Orville Nix's film seemed to show a man aiming a rifle from the roof of a vehicle behind the knoll wall.

primer.name: Eyewitness theories
primer.claim: Of 121 witnesses in the Commission's volumes, Feldman counted 51 who thought shots came from the knoll, 32 from the Depository and 38 with no clear opinion, suggesting two gunmen.
primer.drawback: Eyewitness recollections conflict, so some witnesses must be wrong.

primer.name: Underground man theory
primer.claim: Oswald had no clear motive; the Commission listed five factors (hostility to his surroundings, failure to form relationships, desire for a place in history, Marxism, capacity for decisive action) amounting to blind resentment.

primer.name: Manchurian candidate theory
primer.proponents: Some Commission lawyers and CIA staff
primer.claim: Oswald might have been conditioned in a Soviet hospital as a "sleeper" assassin who was accidentally triggered; the CIA told the Commission this remained a school of thought.

primer.name: Domestic quarrel theory
primer.claim: Oswald, wavering on the eve of the assassination, was rebuffed by Marina and went to the garage for his rifle.

primer.name: Horrible accident theory
primer.claim: Oswald was aiming at Governor Connally, missed, and killed the President by accident.

primer.name: Oedipal theory
primer.proponents: Dr. Renatus Hartogs, who evaluated Oswald at 13
primer.claim: Repressed feelings toward his mother drove Oswald, who fired three times at both Kennedy and Tippit.
primer.drawback: Sylvia Meagher noted Tippit was shot four times, undermining the argument.

primer.name: Killer-instinct theory
primer.claim: Oswald killed two men and tried to shoot at least three others (Connally, Walker and the arresting officer), showing a pattern of violence.
primer.drawback: The idea was dropped by the time the report was written.

primer.name: Planted-rifle theory
primer.claim: A 7.65 German Mauser was found in the Depository and Oswald's Mannlicher-Carcano substituted later; officers first described the rifle as a Mauser.
primer.drawback: Fragments in the limousine ballistically match the Carcano, so it was used in the shooting wherever it was found.

primer.name: Planted-bullet theory
primer.proponents: Richard Popkin, Josiah Thompson, Sylvia Meagher, Vincent Salandria, Léo Sauvage, Harold Weisberg, Mark Lane, Ray Marcus
primer.claim: The nearly whole "stretcher bullet" was fired from Oswald's rifle before the assassination and planted at Parkland to frame him.

primer.name: Oswald impersonator theory
primer.proponents: Léo Sauvage, Harold Weisberg, Sylvia Meagher
primer.claim: Before the assassination someone posing as Oswald planted incriminating clues (at a rifle range, a gunsmith, Mexico City) and probably took part in the shooting.

primer.name: Fall-guy theory
primer.claim: A conspiracy of CIA and FBI officers, Army figures and reactionary oil millionaires used Oswald as a decoy while the killers escaped; the FBI completed the frame-up.

primer.name: Bogus Secret Service man theory
primer.claim: Dallas officer J.M. Smith met a man behind the knoll who showed Secret Service credentials, yet no agent was in that area; the man may have been an escaping gunman.

primer.name: Trunk theory
primer.claim: Muddy footprints behind the picket fence led to parked cars and stopped; a gunman may have hidden in a trunk or stashed the rifle there.

primer.name: Storm drain theory
primer.claim: A storm drain visible in a photo of the knoll later disappeared from photographs, suggesting an escape route that was filled in.

primer.name: Oswald as FBI informer
primer.proponents: Reporter Alonzo Hudkins (via Secret Service report 767)
primer.claim: Oswald was said to be paid $200 a month as FBI informant "S-172"; the Commission never called the sources, and other contacts with FBI agents are cited.
primer.drawback: Hoover categorically denied any connection and offered the FBI's file, which Chief Justice Warren declined.

primer.name: Oswald as secret agent
primer.claim: Oswald was a CIA agent, or (Mailer) an undercover agent for several intelligence services at once.

primer.name: Two Oswalds theory
primer.claim: Witnesses who saw "Oswald" where he couldn't have been saw a look-alike; the real Oswald was a decoy while the double fired the shots.
primer.drawback: The sightings came before anyone knew Kennedy would be in Dallas, which makes a planned deception hard to sustain.

primer.name: Post-assassination domino theory
primer.claim: Witnesses and others connected to the case died under suspicious circumstances because they knew too much.
primer.drawback: Most of the people listed weren't witnesses and few deaths were mysterious (see the Reitzes summary).

primer.name: Racist theory
primer.claim: Southern racists killed Kennedy to stop his civil-rights program and framed a leftist; Oswald's own murder was a separate Dallas police plot.

primer.name: Cui bono theory
primer.proponents: Izvestia, Trud, Joachim Joesten, Barbara Garson, Don B. Reynolds, Jack Ruby and others
primer.claim: Asking who benefited points to Lyndon Johnson.
primer.drawback: No hard evidence; Hoover wrote that he had no information implicating Johnson or Connally.

primer.name: Dallas oligarchy theory
primer.claim: A right-wing Texas oil millionaire had Kennedy killed so Khrushchev would be blamed; Oswald was to be killed by Tippit, and Ruby silenced him when that failed.

primer.name: Cuba-framed theory
primer.claim: The conspirators meant to blame Cuba; Oswald's pro-Castro activity and Mexico City visa attempt laid a false trail to Havana.

primer.name: Crystal ball theory
primer.claim: A psychic "reading" that Castro arranged the killing with Oswald as triggerman.

primer.name: Mafia theory
primer.claim: Chicago organized crime ordered the killing to forestall a crackdown, with Ruby arranging it and Oswald as rifleman.

primer.name: Junta theory
primer.claim: A cabal of the CIA, the Air Force, defense contractors and members of Congress, led by senior officers, eliminated Kennedy after the 1963 Test Ban Treaty.

primer.name: Red execution theory
primer.claim: Moscow ordered Oswald to kill Kennedy, who was about to turn on the Communists.

primer.name: Evil-forces theory
primer.proponents: Ousman Ba, foreign minister of Mali
primer.claim: The same forces behind the deaths of Lumumba and Hammarskjöld killed Kennedy (no details given).

primer.name: The second-thought autopsy report
primer.proponents: Arlen Specter and other Commission lawyers
primer.claim: Specter explained the FBI–autopsy conflict as a tentative autopsy conclusion (the back bullet fell out) later revised.
primer.drawback: Contradicts the Warren Report's own account of the autopsy, which Specter wrote.

primer.name: The Hoover Hegelian theory
primer.claim: Hoover held there was no conflict between the FBI's "finger length" back wound and the autopsy's exit through the throat, only a difference in reporting.
primer.drawback: The two accounts can't both be true.

primer.name: View from the bridge theory
primer.claim: Photographing from S.M. Holland's position, Schiller argued the "smoke" witnesses may have seen something in line with the Depository, not the knoll.
primer.drawback: Holland could likely tell the knoll from a building far beyond it, and other witnesses also reported smoke.

primer.name: The noble lie theory
primer.proponents: Drew Pearson, Henri Nannen (Der Stern), Jacob Cohen
primer.claim: The autopsy findings were held back to hide Kennedy's Addison's disease.
primer.drawback: His Addison's disease was already public, and Robert Kennedy approved giving the materials to the Commission.

primer.name: Manchester theory
primer.claim: Only two shots were fired; the third shell was left over and the many "three shots" witnesses heard echoes.
primer.drawback: Over a hundred witnesses heard more than two shots, some saw a bullet strike the pavement, and Tague was wounded far from the car.

primer.name: Connally's small-detail theory
primer.claim: Connally said he was hit by a different bullet from Kennedy but called it a small detail and urged faith in the Commission.

primer.name: Russell Long theory
primer.claim: Oswald took part, but whoever fired the second shot was a better marksman than Oswald.

primer.name: Shot-through-the-tree theory
primer.claim: A gap in the oak tree's foliage at frames 185–186 allowed an earlier first shot, rescuing the single-gunman theory without the single bullet.
primer.drawback: The gap lasted about a tenth of a second.

primer.name: Steroid theory
primer.claim: Steroids for Addison's disease might have delayed Kennedy's visible reaction to the first shot, supporting an earlier hit.
primer.drawback: Whether he was on steroids was never established.

primer.name: Riddle–Newton theory
primer.claim: Newton's second law says the head should move with the bullet, so a backward lurch means a shot from the front.
primer.drawback: The primer answers with sarcasm only; later experts attributed the motion to a neuromuscular reaction (see the Reitzes summary).

primer.name: Double head-shot theory
primer.proponents: Josiah Thompson and Ray Marcus, independently
primer.claim: The fatal head wound came from two nearly simultaneous shots, from the rear and the right front.

primer.name: Mark Lane's French five-shot theory
primer.claim: Five bullets: two hit Kennedy from behind and in front, one hit Connally, one wounded Tague, and a fifth from the knoll hit the head.
primer.drawback: A bullet entering the throat from the front has no exit wound to explain it.

primer.name: Dal-Tex theory
primer.claim: Shots may have come from the Dal-Tex Building across the street, based on enlarged photos of a fire escape and a window.

primer.name: The 24 frames-per-second theory
primer.claim: If Zapruder's camera ran at 24 frames per second rather than 18.3, the shooting window was shorter than the Commission's 5.6 seconds.
primer.drawback: The FBI timed the camera against a clock, and the manufacturer confirmed its speed.

primer.name: Induced cancer theory
primer.proponents: Jack Ruby, Mark Lane, Penn Jones Jr., Norman Mailer
primer.claim: Ruby's death from cancer was induced by the conspirators to silence him.

primer.name: Two-men-in-a-window theory
primer.claim: She told the FBI she saw a rifleman and a second man in a Depository window; the Commission never evaluated her statement.
primer.drawback: The adjacent window was closed (retort: the second man could have been a lookout).

primer.name: Doctored photograph theory
primer.proponents: Mark Lane, Harold Weisberg, David Lifton and others
primer.claim: The backyard photos of Oswald with the weapons are composites of his head on another body; publications retouched them differently.

primer.name: False knoll theory
primer.claim: Conspirators on and around the knoll used camouflage, explaining why nothing was found there.
primer.drawback: The photo enlargements are extremely grainy and open to interpretation, as Lifton admits.

primer.name: Blunderbuss theory
primer.claim: Several witnesses saw a puff of smoke; if Oswald used an antiquated rifle, a second gunman might have used an even older, smoky weapon.

primer.name: Making of the President theory
primer.claim: Word aboard Air Force One that there was "no conspiracy," before any investigation, was the first sign of a cover-up by powerful people.
primer.drawback: The exact message and its origin are unknown.

primer.name: The I-murder theory
primer.claim: Oswald, a confused double agent, killed Kennedy in a trance-like state for intelligence's own sake.

primer.name: The sugar theory
primer.claim: Seen with a Coke after the shooting, Oswald was a "sugar drunkard" whose brain was confused.

primer.name: The washing-machine theory
primer.claim: An argument over Marina's demand for a washing machine provoked Oswald to lash out.
primer.drawback: Oswald had the materials for the rifle bag before that visit, and they lived near a laundromat.

primer.name: Kennedy lives theory
primer.claim: Tippit was substituted for Kennedy in the limousine, and Kennedy survived in secret.

primer.name: The "what have we here!" theory
primer.claim: Bizarre parallels between the assassination and Benjamin Franklin, Sherlock Holmes, Mormon doctrine and American history; cited as an extreme example of theorizing.
